issues.quote: It is a minute repeater, so when you press the slide it speaks the time. The hours come in low notes. Each quarter is a doubled note. The minutes past the quarter come in high notes.
issues.fact: The fact sheet says nothing about a repeater or how its chimes encode the time. The only sound-based facts are the piano start and stop readings on the kitchen clock.
issues.misreading: A solver could read this as a decoding key for a sounded time, suggesting that a chime heard somewhere gives a reading the sheet never states. That is an invented mechanism, not a fact.

issues.quote: He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century. He used to say that a watch which cannot tell the truth about the time has no business on anyone's wrist.
issues.fact: Not in the fact sheet. It adds an unsupported claim about the watch's purpose and a date-like hint.
issues.misreading: A solver could take the 'new century' remark as a hint about a specific moment or a time-related target the sheet does not give.

issues.quote: Madame plays well. I have heard her many times, and I know the sound of her hands on the keys.
issues.fact: The sheet says only that Madame's piano began and stopped at the stated kitchen readings. It does not say who was playing or that the witness recognised her playing.
issues.misreading: A solver could take this as confirmation that Madame herself was at the piano during the 10:48 to 11:01 window, which the sheet does not establish.

issues.quote: She keeps it that way on purpose, so that nothing in her kitchen is ever late.
issues.fact: The sheet says only that Rosa's clock was exactly fifteen minutes fast. It gives no reason for this.
issues.misreading: The added intent makes the fast offset look deliberate and reliable, which goes beyond the stated fact and could affect how a solver weighs that clock's readings.
